h1: Fast Tracking vs Crashing: Differences and Worked Example
seo_title: Fast Tracking vs Crashing: Differences and Worked Example
meta_description: Fast tracking vs crashing compared: definitions, crash cost slope, a worked example with risk-adjusted cost, break-even rework probability and how to choose.
excerpt: Fast tracking and crashing compared: PMI definitions, a side-by-side table, how each works, the crash cost slope, and an illustrative six-activity ICT refurbishment example that compares crash-only, fast-track-only and blended options on expected and worst-case cost, with break-even rework probabilities and a probability-impact screen for choosing.
learning_objectives: Define fast tracking, crashing and schedule compression per the PMI Lexicon
Compare the techniques on cost, risk, predictability, reversibility, resources and float
Calculate crash cost slopes and crash the critical path cheapest-first
Cost fast-tracking risk with EMV and compare options on expected and worst-case cost
Compute a break-even rework probability and use it to test the decision
Record and approve the chosen option through the risk register, change control and baseline

formulas.formula: Crash cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal duration − crash duration)
formulas.variables: costs in $; durations in working days; result $/day

formulas.formula: Path length = sum of durations; forward pass with FS-lead on B→D
formulas.inputs: A3 B4 C3 D5 E2 F2
formulas.result: A-B-D-F 14, A-C-E-F 10; crash D2+B1 → 11 for $5,000; FS-3d → D starts day 5, finish 11; crash D1 + FS-2d → D starts day 6, finish 11; float on A-C-E-F 4 → 1

formulas.formula: EMV of rework = P × (rework cost + delay days × daily late cost); expected total = direct cost + EMV
formulas.variables: P decimal; costs $; delay days working days; late cost $2,500/day

formulas.formula: Break-even P = (crash-only cost − blend direct cost) ÷ rework impact
